entities.name: Richard de Beauchamp, 1st Earl of Worcester
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard de Beauchamp, 1st Earl of Worcester (c. 1397 – 18 March 1422), was a prominent English nobleman and military commander whose brief but impactful career unfolded during the tumultuous zenith of the Hundred Years' War. As a scion of one of England's most powerful baronial families, the Beauchamps of Warwick, his trajectory was intimately linked to the Lancastrian monarchy and its ambitious campaigns in France under King Henry V. His elevation to an earldom, a rare distinction, underscored his military contributions and the Crown's strategic need for loyal, capable leaders in a period of aggressive expansion and intense Anglo-French conflict, making him a representative figure of the martial aristocracy of early 15th-century England.

Beauchamp inherited the barony of Bergavenny (now Abergavenny) in 1411 upon the death of his father, William de Beauchamp, 1st Baron Bergavenny. His military service began early, leading to his knighting as a Knight of the Bath in 1413 at the coronation of King Henry V. He distinguished himself in the English campaigns in France, notably participating in the pivotal Siege of Rouen from July 1418 to January 1419, a strategic victory that secured Normandy for the English. His valor and loyalty were further recognized when he was created Earl of Worcester on 16 December 1421, a new creation of the earldom, making him one of the few individuals to hold such a title during Henry V's reign.

His promising career was tragically cut short when he died from a cannon shot during the protracted Siege of Meaux on 18 March 1422, fighting alongside King Henry V. The Earldom of Worcester became extinct upon his death, as he left only a daughter, Elizabeth de Beauchamp, who inherited the Barony of Bergavenny. His death, occurring just five months before King Henry V's own demise, symbolized the high cost of the Lancastrian ambitions in France and the personal sacrifices made by the English nobility in pursuit of a dual monarchy.
